meta.title: "Do it or you'll fail everything": when a chain of events sounds logical but is unchecked | Sila Slova
meta.description: Teach your child to break "logical" chains into steps and check each one: does one really lead to the next? Game-based critical thinking course for children aged 8–12.

hero.headline: Does your child believe a "logical story" without checking the steps?
hero.subheadline: "Do it or you'll get a bad grade, then fail everything." "Go or you'll lose your chance, and it'll never come again." Each step sounds fine — but nobody checks whether it actually leads to the next.

media.alt: A child taking a chain of events as fact without checking each step

pain.title: This isn't logic — it's a chain with no checking
pain.body:
Events are lined up one after another, and it feels inevitable: "A → so B → so C → catastrophe". It sounds coherent, so it's easy to believe. But between the steps there are often gaps where nothing is proven: "a bad grade" doesn't mean "you'll fail everything", "one chance" doesn't mean "never again".

This isn't believing everything or naivety. The child simply doesn't yet have the habit of breaking a story into parts and questioning each link separately: "does this really follow from the last one?". So they take the whole scenario as one ready-made fact.

The result — the child agrees because of "sort-of logic" that was never actually checked. They rush, refuse, fear consequences that may not even happen — because the chain sounded whole, even though it rested on unproven links.

solution.title: "Sila Slova" — a detective drama that teaches critical thinking
solution.body: 40 episodes, 13 critical thinking lessons. Your child plays — but is actually learning to protect themselves.
bullets: 🔍 Breaks a "logical story" down into separate steps
🧠 Checks each link: "does this really follow from the previous one?"
💬 Spots the gaps where one thing isn't proven to lead to another
🛡️ Doesn't accept the whole chain automatically until they've checked it step by step

social_proof.quote: Any "and then it'll get even worse" used to work on my son instantly. Now he stops: "But why does one definitely lead to the other?" — and often finds for himself where the chain breaks.
social_proof.author: Maryna, mum of 11-year-old Denys

faq.q: Is it a game or a learning course?
faq.a: Both at the same time. "Sila Slova" looks like a detective series, but every episode contains a hidden critical thinking lesson.

faq.q: What age is it suitable for?
faq.a: Ideal for 8–12 year olds. At this age, children are most receptive to new thinking patterns and haven't yet formed rigid biases.

faq.q: How much time is needed each day?
faq.a: 15–20 minutes per episode. Flexible schedule — your child can come back at any convenient time.

faq.q: Is registration required for the demo?
faq.a: No. The demo episode is fully open — no registration, no subscription, no personal data required.
